newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan businessmen urge dialogue after violence.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan businessmen urge dialogue after violence.

text.p: Kenyan business leaders are urging dialogue between opposition groups and the government to end a stalemate over constitutional reforms and help restore confidence in an emerging economy.
"Confidence is a very fragile thing. Any kind of instability hurts investor confidence," said Micah Cheserem, governor of the Central Bank of Kenya. "Dialogue is the key word."

"The main test for Kenya is that the nation holds together -- to give confidence that this is a good place to invest," said Chris Kirubi, a leading businessman with interests ranging from real estate to cosmetics manufacturing and express mail delivery.

Nine people died in unrest last Monday when opposition groups called rallies to put pressure on President Daniel arap Moi to institute reforms before general elections due later this year. They defied Moi's order banning demonstrations.
Further violence erupted on Wednesday when university students were sent home after clashing with police and paramilitary forces.

The opposition, backed by churches, students and human rights groups, wants Moi to allow free access to the media, overhaul of the state-appointed Electoral Commission and repeal of a colonial-era act that regulates political assemblies.

The opposition, normally divided on personal and tribal lines, got a lift on Saturday with the return from two years of forced exile in Germany of a fiery Moslem preacher and Moi critic, Sheikh Khalid Balala.
On Friday the Kenyan shilling recouped heavy losses which followed the riots, after the Central Bank unloaded $29 million to counter an outflow of cash.

One commercial bank that bid 61.50 shillings to the dollar early on Friday adjusted its offer to 58.60 at the day's close. Cheserem said the central bank was standing by to meet any demand on Monday but indications were that pressure on the forex market was easing.

"The president must listen to the people. The government won praise for major economic reforms after the 1992 elections. A perception that the question of political reforms will drag on reduces confidence in the system," said Betty Maina, executive director at the independent Institute of Economic Affairs.

At a weekend rally, Moi hinted he was prepared to discuss opposition demands with key organisations in his ruling KANU party, but did not fix a date for such discussions. No date for elections has yet been set.
Kirubi, who has close links with Kenya's leadership, told Reuters the government was "prepared to make sure that the situation does not deteriorate", adding: "That will calm markets".

Kirubi said Kenya's leading foreign exchange earner, tourism, faced a threat because "tourists only go to places where there is peace". Kenya's top commodity exports, tea and coffee, are threatened by unfavourable weather.
He said business wanted to expand manufacturing and create jobs because unemployment was one of Kenya's biggest headaches.
Some 46 percent of Kenya's 29 million people live below the poverty line and per capita income is $283, according to official statistics.
